summary: Archives the report of the joint IETF and ITU-T working team on applying MPLS to transport networks. The team recommended that the two organizations work together, bringing transport requirements into the IETF and extending MPLS forwarding, OAM, survivability, network management, and control plane protocols to meet them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two groups were building roads in the same land. This is the report where they agreed to work together on one set of roads instead of two incompatible ones.

questions: why did ietf and itu-t work together on mpls
what did the joint working team recommend
subtitle: How the IETF and ITU-T agreed to build MPLS for transport networks

tldr.problem: The ITU-T (a United Nations telecommunications group) was designing T-MPLS, an incompatible variant of MPLS for transport networks, which threatened interoperability between the Internet and transport networks.
tldr.mechanism: IETF leadership challenged this approach, proposing two options: either work together on a single MPLS-based solution or create completely separate incompatible protocols. A Joint Working Team studied both options and recommended working together.
tldr.outcome: Both organizations agreed on Option 1: the IETF and ITU-T would collaborate to extend IETF MPLS (calling it MPLS-TP) to meet transport network requirements, ensuring architectural compatibility.

facts.label: Key recommendation
facts.value: Option 1: Extend IETF MPLS for transport use (MPLS-TP)

facts.label: Outcome
facts.value: Both ITU-T and IETF accepted the recommendation

today: RFC 5317 is an Informational document published in February 2009 that archives the JWT report. The MPLS-TP work that followed from this agreement resulted in multiple RFCs defining the Transport Profile for MPLS, which is now deployed in operational transport networks alongside IETF MPLS in Internet networks.

sections.title: Background and the Problem
sections.content:
For several years, the ITU-T (the International Telecommunications Union's standardization arm) had been developing a protocol called T-MPLS for use in transport networks—the core networks that provide wide-area connectivity for services like IP and telephony.

The ITU-T based T-MPLS on MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), an IETF-standardized protocol. However, the two organizations made incompatible design choices. By the time IETF leadership became aware of the incompatibilities, the ITU-T was far along in its standardization process. IETF leadership concluded that this incompatibility would be a "mutual danger to both the Internet and the Transport network," potentially causing serious interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone standards group was building something based on an Internet standard, but in a way that would not work with the Internet version.

sections.title: The Two Options
sections.content:
IETF leadership issued a liaison statement offering two paths forward. Option 1 was for T-MPLS to become a fully compliant MPLS protocol, standardized under the IETF process as an extension to MPLS. Option 2 was for T-MPLS to become a completely disjoint protocol with a new name and entirely new code points, unrelated to IETF MPLS.

The ITU-T proposed forming a Joint Working Team (JWT) to analyze these options and make a recommendation. The JWT included experts from both organizations and had support from an IETF Design Team and an ITU-T Ad Hoc Group on T-MPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF said: either work with us to make one road system together, or build a completely different one.

sections.title: Technical Feasibility Analysis
sections.content:
The JWT divided the analysis into five areas: forwarding, OAM (Operations, Administration, and Management), protection and survivability, control plane, and network management.

For each area, the team examined whether Option 1—extending IETF MPLS to meet transport network requirements—was technically feasible. The analysis covered forwarding mechanisms, OAM hierarchies, label-switched path monitoring, the Associated Channel Header for carrying OAM traffic, control plane protocols, survivability scenarios like link and node protection, and network management requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The team studied each part of the system to see if it could be made to work.

sections.title: The MPLS-TP Architecture
sections.content:
The JWT concluded that the existing IETF MPLS architecture could be extended to meet transport network requirements through what became known as the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP).

Key findings included that MPLS forwarding required no changes, that OAM could work through extensions using the Associated Channel Header mechanism, that existing IETF control plane protocols like GMPLS could be extended to meet transport requirements, and that existing protection and survivability mechanisms could be adapted.
sections.plainLanguage: The team found that the IETF version of MPLS could be extended to do everything the transport group needed.

sections.title: Recommendation and Outcome
sections.content:
The JWT unanimously recommended Option 1, concluding that there were no "show stopper" technical issues preventing this approach. Both organizations accepted this recommendation, establishing a path for collaboration.

The JWT recommended that MPLS-TP be defined through the normal IETF standards process and published in RFCs. The ITU-T would develop recommendations for integrating MPLS-TP into transport equipment and networks, align its existing T-MPLS recommendations with MPLS-TP, and make normative references to the appropriate RFCs. The MPLS Interoperability Design Team and related groups would continue to facilitate information exchange and coordinate the work.
sections.plainLanguage: Both groups agreed to work together and use one set of standards, with the Internet group handling the core definitions and the phone group handling the integration.

sections.title: Significance and Impact
sections.content:
This agreement was significant because it avoided a potential fragmentation of the Internet and transport network infrastructure. Rather than creating incompatible protocols that would need translation and bridging, the two organizations committed to a unified technical direction.

The JWT recommendations were archived in RFC 5317, with the full report available as PowerPoint slides in the PDF version. The agreement established a precedent for how IETF and ITU-T could collaborate on standards affecting both the Internet and telecommunications infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of two groups building two different things that could not talk to each other, they agreed to work together.
